intro: In 1324 a king from West Africa rode into Cairo with so much gold that prices fell and stayed down for years. In 1348 a cart rolled into an English village and, within a season, half its people were dead of plague. Both events happened because the world between 500 and 1500 was connected by roads, rivers, oceans and deserts that people had learned to cross. Goods moved along those routes. So did faiths, numbers, books and germs.

This unit follows those routes. You will start in Constantinople, the city that kept Rome alive for a thousand years, and in Mecca and Baghdad, where a new religion built an empire and a library. You will cross the Sahara by camel to the gold kingdoms of Ghana and Mali, and sail the monsoon winds to the stone cities of Zimbabwe and the Swahili coast. Then you will turn to the castles and cathedrals of Europe, the horsemen of Genghis Khan, the samurai of Japan, and the pyramids, floating farms and mountain roads of the Maya, Aztec and Inca.

Along the way you will practice reading history the way historians do: from a traveler's report, a law code, a tribute list, a coin dug out of a wall. By the end you will be able to explain how faith, law and trade held big societies together, what happened when disaster struck, and why the world of 1450 was ready to collide.
bigQuestion: Between 500 and 1500, how did faith, law and trade connect the world's great societies, and who paid the price of that connection?

timeline.t: Constantine makes Constantinople the capital of the eastern Roman Empire
Justinian's lawyers finish organizing Roman law into one code
Muhammad and his followers move from Mecca to Medina, year one of the Muslim calendar
The Abbasids found Baghdad, soon home to the House of Wisdom
Temujin unites the Mongol tribes and is named Genghis Khan
King John seals Magna Carta at Runnymede
Mansa Musa of Mali passes through Cairo on his pilgrimage to Mecca
The Aztec found Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco
The Inca of Cusco begin building the largest empire in the Americas
The Ottoman Turks take Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire

words.d: the eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople from 330 to 1453
a complete, organized set of laws written down in one place
a ruler of the Muslim community after Muhammad; the word means successor
a journey to a holy place for religious reasons
a group of traders and pack animals traveling together for safety
a wind that blows one way for half the year and the opposite way for the other half
the medieval system in which lords gave land in exchange for loyalty and military service
a farmer bound to a lord's land, who could not leave it
a deadly disease that spreads fast through a population; the Black Death was bubonic plague
a written document that grants or guarantees rights
goods that a conquered people must pay to their rulers
an Inca record made of knotted strings, used to keep numbers

test.q: Why was Constantinople so hard to conquer and so easy to make rich?
choices: It sat on a strait with water on three sides, where all ships had to pass
It sat far inland behind mountains
It had no walls but a huge army
It was the birthplace of Islam
test.why: Its location on the strait gave it defense and a tax on every passing ship.

test.q: What did Justinian's Code do for Roman law?
choices: Sorted, trimmed and organized a thousand years of it into one set of books
test.why: Tribonian's team produced the Body of Civil Law between 529 and 534.

test.q: Which duties did Islam ask of every Muslim, rich or poor?
choices: Building a mosque and a school
Prayer, giving to the poor, fasting, pilgrimage and the declaration of faith
test.why: The five duties were the same for everyone, which was part of the faith's appeal.

test.q: What was the House of Wisdom?
choices: A center in Baghdad where scholars translated and studied the world's knowledge
test.why: Under al-Ma'mun in the 800s, scholars gathered Greek, Persian and Indian works and built on them.

test.q: Why was salt worth gold south of the Sahara?
choices: The region had almost no salt, and people cannot live without it
Salt was used as money in Mali
Salt was needed to make gold coins
test.why: Salt from desert mines like Taghaza filled a real need, so traders exchanged it for gold.

test.q: How do historians know about the kingdom of Ghana?
choices: From Arab writers like al-Bakri and from archaeology at Koumbi Saleh
test.why: Ghana left no surviving writing, so outside accounts and digs are the main evidence.

test.q: What do the objects found at Great Zimbabwe show?
choices: The city was built by Phoenicians
The city had a written language
The city traded with the Indian Ocean world
The city was a Roman colony
test.why: Chinese porcelain, Persian pottery, Indian beads and a Kilwa coin prove long-distance trade.

test.q: In feudal Europe, what did a serf owe the lord?
choices: A tenth of income to the pope
Labor on the lord's land and a share of the crop
test.why: Serfs worked the lord's fields several days a week and gave part of their harvest in return for protection.

test.q: Which was an effect of the crusades that no one planned?
choices: Italian cities grew rich and Arabic learning reached Europe
Europe cut off all trade with Asia
test.why: Venice and Genoa profited, and scholars brought back books on math, medicine and philosophy.

test.q: How did the Black Death travel from Asia to Europe?
choices: Through the air across the ocean
Along the trade routes, by caravan and ship
test.why: Fleas on rats and people rode the Mongol-era trade routes to the Black Sea and then to Sicily in 1347.

test.q: What did Magna Carta establish in 1215?
choices: That the king rules under the law, not above it
test.why: The barons forced King John to accept limits on taxes and on jailing men without lawful judgment.

test.q: Which statement about the Mongol Empire is true?
choices: It was the largest connected land empire in history and made Asian roads safer for trade
test.why: From Korea to Hungary, Mongol rule brought both massacres and a century of easier travel.

test.q: How was a Japanese samurai similar to a European knight?
choices: Both served a lord in exchange for land and followed a code of honor
Both were paid in paper money
test.why: Two societies with no contact built similar systems of warriors bound to lords.

test.q: Which people built chinampas, raised fields in a lake, to feed their capital?
test.why: Tenochtitlan sat in Lake Texcoco, and chinampas gave several harvests a year.

test.q: What did the Inca use to keep records?
choices: Quipus, knotted strings that recorded numbers
test.why: The Inca had no writing; officials read numbers from the knots on colored strings.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Between 500 and 1500, did trade do more to help people or to harm them? Use evidence from both chapters, such as the trans-Saharan gold and salt trade, the House of Wisdom, the Swahili coast, the Mongol roads, the Black Death and the slave trades, to support your claim.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence: trade mostly helped, mostly harmed, or both in ways you can name.
Use at least three pieces of evidence from the unit, such as Mansa Musa in Cairo, the numerals that reached Europe from India, or the plague riding the trade routes.
Explain your reasoning: say why each piece of evidence supports your claim, not just what happened.
Give the other side a fair sentence. What would someone who disagrees point to?
End by saying who gained the most and who paid the most, and how you know.
